claim: The superior colliculus (SC) is a midbrain structure implicated in early sensorimotor transformation.
source: Here, we performed high-throughput and circuit-specific single-cell transcriptomic analyses of neurons in the superior colliculus (SC), a midbrain structure implicated in early sensorimotor transformation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established knowledge about the SC's role.

claim: SC neurons in distinct laminae expressed discrete marker genes.
source: We found that SC neurons in distinct laminae expressed discrete marker genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cbln2 and Pitx2 are key markers that define glutamatergic projection neurons in the optic nerve (Op) and intermediate gray (InG) layers, respectively.
source: Of particular interest, Cbln2 and Pitx2 were key markers that define glutamatergic projection neurons in the optic nerve (Op) and intermediate gray (InG) layers, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptomic and anatomical data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Cbln2+ neurons responded to visual stimuli mimicking cruising predators.
source: The Cbln2+ neurons responded to visual stimuli mimicking cruising predators, while the Pitx2+ neurons encoded prey-derived vibrissal tactile cues.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4.

claim: Pitx2+ neurons encoded prey-derived vibrissal tactile cues.
source: The Cbln2+ neurons responded to visual stimuli mimicking cruising predators, while the Pitx2+ neurons encoded prey-derived vibrissal tactile cues.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4.

claim: Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ neuronal subtypes form distinct input and output connections with other brain areas.
source: By forming distinct input and output connections with other brain areas, these neuronal subtypes independently mediated behaviors of predator avoidance and prey capture.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by rabies virus tracing and AAV tracing data in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ neuronal subtypes independently mediated behaviors of predator avoidance and prey capture.
source: By forming distinct input and output connections with other brain areas, these neuronal subtypes independently mediated behaviors of predator avoidance and prey capture.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data with TeNT inactivation and optogenetic activation in Figures 3 and 8.

claim: In the midbrain, sensorimotor transformation for different behaviors may be performed by separate circuit modules that are molecularly defined by distinct transcriptomic codes.
source: Our results reveal that, in the midbrain, sensorimotor transformation for different behaviors may be performed by separate circuit modules that are molecularly defined by distinct transcriptomic codes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on integration of transcriptomic, anatomical, and behavioral data.

claim: Sensorimotor transformation is a fundamental process in which the brain converts sensory information into motor command.
source: Sensorimotor transformation is a fundamental process in which the brain converts sensory information into motor command (Crochet et al., 2019; Franklin and Wolpert, 2011; Pouget and Snyder, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The critical role of sensorimotor transformation in sensory-guided behaviors has been demonstrated in diverse animal models, including fish, rodents, and primates.
source: The critical role of this process in sensory-guided behaviors has been demonstrated in diverse animal models, including fish (Bianco and Engert, 2015; Chen et al., 2018; Helmbrecht et al., 2018), rodents (Felsen and Mainen, 2008; Huda et al., 2020; Mayrhofer et al., 2019; Oliveira and Yonehara, 2018; Wang et al., 2020a), and primates (Buneo et al., 2002; Cavanaugh et al., 2012; Sparks, 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations across different species.

claim: The molecular and genetic logic behind sensorimotor transformation remains elusive.
source: Although the brain circuits and computational models of sensorimotor transformation have been intensively studied, the molecular and genetic logic behind this process remains elusive.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) are powerful approaches to identify the genes expressed in individual cells.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) are powerful approaches to identify the genes expressed in individual cells (Liu et al., 2020; Shapiro et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2009; Zhong et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2018), enabling us to understand the cellular diversity and gene expression profiles of a specific brain region (Economo et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The superficial layers of the SC, including the superficial gray (SuG) layer and the optic nerve (Op) layer, are involved in visual information processing.
source: The superficial layers of the SC, including the superficial gray (SuG) layer and the optic nerve (Op) layer, are involved in visual information processing (De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018; Gale and Murphy, 2014; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The deep layers of the SC, including the intermediate layer and deep layer, participate in processing of tactile and auditory information.
source: The deep layers of the SC, including the intermediate layer and deep layer, participate in processing of tactile and auditory information (Cohen et al., 2008; Dräger and Hubel, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The deep layers of the SC control eye movement, head movement, and locomotion.
source: The deep layers of the SC control eye movement (Sparks, 1986; Wang et al., 2015), head movement (Isa and Sasaki, 2002; Wilson et al., 2018), and locomotion (Felsen and Mainen, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The sensorimotor transformations that occur in the SC enable it to orchestrate distinct behavioral actions in predator avoidance and prey capture.
source: From a neuroethological perspective, the sensorimotor transformations that occur in the SC enable it to orchestrate distinct behavioral actions in predator avoidance and prey capture (Dean et al., 1989; Oliveira and Yonehara, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: 14,892 single-cell gene expression profiles were collected from mouse SC using snRNA-seq.
source: From two experimental replicates, each containing six superior colliculi, 14,892 single-cell gene expression profiles were collected (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: Nine major types of cells were identified in the SC: excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, ciliated cells, and meningeal cells.
source: In total, we found nine major types of cells identified by the expression of classic marker genes; these were excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, ciliated cells, and meningeal cells (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Excitatory neurons were divided into 9 subclusters and inhibitory neurons into 10 subclusters, each with distinctive transcriptomic profiles.
source: To further investigate neural diversity, we divided the excitatory and inhibitory neurons into 9 and 10 subclusters, respectively, each of which displayed a distinctive transcriptomic profile (Figure 1A,C–D; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Subclusters In-5 and In-10 are Calb1+ and Reln+ interneurons, respectively.
source: The differentially expressed genes (DEGs) expressed by the cells in these subsets indicate that subclusters In-5 and In-10 are Calb1+ and Reln+ interneurons, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of DEGs shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cells of subsets Ex-5/7/8/9 and In-2/7/8/10 were assigned to the SuG matter layer.
source: Cells of subsets Ex-5/7/8/9 and In-2/7/8/10 were assigned to the SuG matter layer, while cells in the Ex-3/6 and In-3 subsets localized in the Op layer.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPACED spatial classification method applied to the snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cells in the Ex-3/6 and In-3 subsets localized in the Op layer.
source: Cells of subsets Ex-5/7/8/9 and In-2/7/8/10 were assigned to the SuG matter layer, while cells in the Ex-3/6 and In-3 subsets localized in the Op layer.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPACED spatial classification method applied to the snRNA-seq data.

claim: Ex-1/4 and In-4 cells exhibited high spatial scores for the intermediate gray and white (InG/InWh) layers.
source: In addition, Ex-1/4 and In-4 cells exhibited high spatial scores for the intermediate gray and white (InG/InWh) layers (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) (p < 0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the SPACED spatial classification method with statistical significance.

claim: GO terms suggest that predicted SuG layer cells may play roles in visual learning and cognition.
source: Intriguingly, the GO terms suggest that predicted SuG layer cells may play roles in visual learning and cognition, consistent with previous findings that cells in this layer receive signals from the retina and the visual cortex (Sparks, 1986).
evidence: This is an inference from GO analysis supported by citation to previous work.

claim: GO analysis indicated that cells predicted in the Op layer may be involved in defense and fear responses.
source: The GO analysis also indicated that cells that are predicted in the Op layer may be involved in defense and fear responses, while cells that are predicted in the InG layer may play roles in locomotor behavior (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an inference from GO analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: GO analysis indicated that cells predicted in the InG layer may play roles in locomotor behavior.
source: The GO analysis also indicated that cells that are predicted in the Op layer may be involved in defense and fear responses, while cells that are predicted in the InG layer may play roles in locomotor behavior (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an inference from GO analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: One neuron with a cell body in the Op layer and dendritic ramifications in the SuG and Op layers extended its axon in the lateral posterior thalamic nucleus (LPTN).
source: One neuron with a cell body in the Op layer and dendritic ramifications in the SuG and Op layers extended its axon in the lateral posterior thalamic nucleus (LPTN).
evidence: This is a finding from morphological reconstruction shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Another neuron showed dendrites restricted to InG/InWh layer and a branched axon reaching the zona incerta (ZI).
source: Another neuron showed dendrites restricted to InG/InWh layer and a branched axon reaching the zona incerta (ZI) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from morphological reconstruction shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Retrogradely labeled EGFP+ SC neurons projecting to LPTN were predominantly localized within the Op layer.
source: Retrogradely labeled EGFP+ SC neurons were predominantly localized within the Op layer (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from retrograde tracing shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ZI-projecting SC neurons are distributed in the InG/InWh and deep gray (DpG) layers of the SC.
source: With a similar strategy, we labeled ZI-projecting SC neurons with EGFP; these neurons are distributed in the InG/InWh and deep gray (DpG) layers of the SC (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is a finding from retrograde tracing shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: LPTN-projecting and ZI-projecting SC neurons did not show significant differences in resting membrane potential.
source: These two populations of SC projection neurons did not show significant differences in resting membrane potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) or firing threshold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LPTN-projecting and ZI-projecting SC neurons did not show significant differences in firing threshold.
source: These two populations of SC projection neurons did not show significant differences in resting membrane potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) or firing threshold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The number of action potentials fired by LPTN-projecting and ZI-projecting neurons in response to membrane depolarization did not show a significant difference.
source: The number of action potentials fired by LPTN-projecting and ZI-projecting neurons in response to membrane depolarization also did not show a significant difference (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: LPTN-projecting and ZI-projecting neurons are similar in their electrophysiological properties and cannot be distinguished using traditional electrophysiological measurements.
source: These data suggest that LPTN-projecting and ZI-projecting neurons are similar in their electrophysiological properties and that they cannot be distinguished using traditional electrophysiological measurements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: 60 cells were collected for patch-seq experiments, including 21 LPTN-projecting neurons from the Op layer and 39 ZI-projecting neurons from the InG layer.
source: In total, 78 cells were collected; 60 of these cells, including 21 LPTN-projecting neurons from the Op layer and 39 ZI-projecting neurons from the InG layer, passed the quality control test, with a median number of 7746 genes expressed per cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental data collected.

claim: Neurons with different projections were clustered separately based on gene expression.
source: Examination of classic markers indicated that these cells were vGlut-expressing neurons and the neurons with different projections were clustered separately (Figure 2H), indicating that neurons with the same circuit connections may have similar innate gene expression profiles.
evidence: This is a finding from patch-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Neurons with the same circuit connections may have similar innate gene expression profiles.
source: Examination of classic markers indicated that these cells were vGlut-expressing neurons and the neurons with different projections were clustered separately (Figure 2H), indicating that neurons with the same circuit connections may have similar innate gene expression profiles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering of patch-seq data.

claim: InG layer neurons projecting to ZI highly expressed Pitx2, Vwc2, Gsg1l, Clstn2, and other genes.
source: The InG layer neurons projecting to ZI with soma in the SC highly expressed Pitx2, Vwc2, Gsg1l, Clstn2, and other genes, while LPTN-projecting Op layer neurons highly expressed Cbln2, Grm8, Zfp385b, Dgkh, and other genes (Figure 2I–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–I; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from DEG analysis of patch-seq data shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: LPTN-projecting Op layer neurons highly expressed Cbln2, Grm8, Zfp385b, Dgkh, and other genes.
source: The InG layer neurons projecting to ZI with soma in the SC highly expressed Pitx2, Vwc2, Gsg1l, Clstn2, and other genes, while LPTN-projecting Op layer neurons highly expressed Cbln2, Grm8, Zfp385b, Dgkh, and other genes (Figure 2I–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–I; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from DEG analysis of patch-seq data shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: Op-LPTN neurons identified through patch-seq were similar to cells of the Ex-6 subset in terms of their cellular gene expression profiles.
source: Transcriptomic correlation analysis indicated that Op-LPTN neurons and InG-ZI neurons identified through patch-seq were similar to cells of the Ex-6 and Ex-4 subsets, respectively, in terms of their cellular gene expression profiles (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is a finding from transcriptomic correlation analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: InG-ZI neurons identified through patch-seq were similar to cells of the Ex-4 subset in terms of their cellular gene expression profiles.
source: Transcriptomic correlation analysis indicated that Op-LPTN neurons and InG-ZI neurons identified through patch-seq were similar to cells of the Ex-6 and Ex-4 subsets, respectively, in terms of their cellular gene expression profiles (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is a finding from transcriptomic correlation analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Cbln2 was expressed in both Ex-3 and Ex-6 cells, while Dgkh was only highly expressed in Ex-6 cells.
source: For example, as a marker gene of Op-LPTN projection neurons, Cbln2 was expressed in both Ex-3 and Ex-6 cells, while Dgkh was only highly expressed in Ex-6 cells (Figure 2L,N).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of DEGs shown in Figure 2L and 2N.

claim: Pitx2 was exclusively expressed in Ex-4 neurons, but Vwc2 was expressed in both subsets of neurons.
source: Among genes that were specifically expressed in InG-ZI projection neurons, Pitx2 was exclusively expressed in Ex-4 neurons, but Vwc2 was expressed in both subsets of neurons (Figure 2M–N).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of DEGs shown in Figure 2M and 2N.

claim: The projection-specific SC neurons represent subpopulations of neurons in specific SC layers that can be distinguished by their gene expression profiles.
source: These data suggest that the projection-specific SC neurons represent subpopulations of neurons in specific SC layers that can be distinguished by their gene expression profiles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration of patch-seq and snRNA-seq data.

claim: Cbln2 and Pitx2 displayed the highest fidelity of Op and InG layer specificity based on analysis of in situ RNA hybridization images from Allen Brain Atlas.
source: Cbln2 and Pitx2 were highly expressed in LPTN-projecting and ZI-projecting SC neurons, respectively (Figure 2I), which also displayed the highest fidelity of Op and InG layer specificity based on our analysis of in situ RNA hybridization images from Allen Brain Atlas (https://mouse.brain-map.org) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of Allen Brain Atlas data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: More than 90% of EGFP-expressing SC neurons in Cbln2-IRES-Cre mice were positive for Cbln2 mRNA.
source: More than 90% of EGFP-expressing SC neurons were positive for Cbln2 mRNA (91 ± 9%, n=3 mice), and SC neurons expressing Cbln2 mRNA were predominantly positive for EGFP (92 ± 11%, n=3 mice), suggesting that it is possible to specifically label Cbln2+ neurons in the SC of Cbln2-IRES-Cre mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from validation of the Cbln2-IRES-Cre mouse line shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SC neurons expressing Cbln2 mRNA were predominantly positive for EGFP (92 ± 11%, n=3 mice) in Cbln2-IRES-Cre mice.
source: More than 90% of EGFP-expressing SC neurons were positive for Cbln2 mRNA (91 ± 9%, n=3 mice), and SC neurons expressing Cbln2 mRNA were predominantly positive for EGFP (92 ± 11%, n=3 mice), suggesting that it is possible to specifically label Cbln2+ neurons in the SC of Cbln2-IRES-Cre mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from validation of the Cbln2-IRES-Cre mouse line shown in Figure 3B.

claim: EGFP-expressing SC neurons in Cbln2-IRES-Cre mice were mostly positive for vGlut2 mRNA (93 ± 6%, n=3 mice).
source: In addition, EGFP-expressing SC neurons were mostly positive for vGlut2 mRNA (93 ± 6%, n=3 mice), and very few were positive for vGAT mRNA (4 ± 2.1%, n=3 mice), confirming that the Cbln2+ SC neurons were predominantly glutamatergic (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from validation of the Cbln2-IRES-Cre mouse line shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Very few EGFP-expressing SC neurons in Cbln2-IRES-Cre mice were positive for vGAT mRNA (4 ± 2.1%, n=3 mice).
source: In addition, EGFP-expressing SC neurons were mostly positive for vGlut2 mRNA (93 ± 6%, n=3 mice), and very few were positive for vGAT mRNA (4 ± 2.1%, n=3 mice), confirming that the Cbln2+ SC neurons were predominantly glutamatergic (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from validation of the Cbln2-IRES-Cre mouse line shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons were predominantly glutamatergic.
source: In addition, EGFP-expressing SC neurons were mostly positive for vGlut2 mRNA (93 ± 6%, n=3 mice), and very few were positive for vGAT mRNA (4 ± 2.1%, n=3 mice), confirming that the Cbln2+ SC neurons were predominantly glutamatergic (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the high percentage of vGlut2+ and low percentage of vGAT+ cells.

claim: Mice exhibit a freezing response to an overhead moving visual target under laboratory conditions.
source: Under laboratory conditions, mice exhibit a freezing response to an overhead moving visual target; this is an innate behavior that may be crucial to the avoidance of aerial predators in the natural environment (De Franceschi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Synaptic inactivation of Cbln2+ SC neurons by TeNT strongly impaired visually evoked freezing responses.
source: We found that control mice with Cbln2+ SC neurons expressing EGFP (Ctrl) exhibited freezing in response to an overhead moving visual target (Figure 3—video 1; black trace in Figure 3D). In contrast, synaptic inactivation of Cbln2+ SC neurons by TeNT strongly impaired visually evoked freezing responses (Figure 3—video 1; red trace in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Synaptic inactivation of Cbln2+ SC neurons caused a significant increase in locomotion speed during visual stimuli but not before or after visual stimuli.
source: Quantitative analyses indicated that synaptic inactivation of Cbln2+ SC neurons caused a significant increase in locomotion speed during visual stimuli but not before or after visual stimuli (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: Inactivation of Cbln2+ SC neurons did not alter the efficiency of predatory hunting.
source: However, inactivation of Cbln2+ SC neurons did not alter the efficiency of predatory hunting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-I.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons are selectively required for a visually evoked freezing response in mice.
source: These data suggest that Cbln2+ SC neurons are selectively required for a visually evoked freezing response in mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing impaired freezing but not hunting.

claim: Most EGFP-expressing SC neurons in Pitx2-Cre mice were positive for Pitx2 mRNA (88 ± 8%, n=3 mice).
source: Most EGFP-expressing SC neurons were positive for Pitx2 mRNA (88 ± 8%, n=3 mice), and SC neurons expressing Pitx2 mRNA were predominantly positive for EGFP (89 ± 9%, n=3 mice), suggesting that Pitx2+ SC neurons were specifically labeled in Pitx2-Cre mice (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a finding from validation of the Pitx2-Cre mouse line shown in Figure 3I.

claim: SC neurons expressing Pitx2 mRNA were predominantly positive for EGFP (89 ± 9%, n=3 mice) in Pitx2-Cre mice.
source: Most EGFP-expressing SC neurons were positive for Pitx2 mRNA (88 ± 8%, n=3 mice), and SC neurons expressing Pitx2 mRNA were predominantly positive for EGFP (89 ± 9%, n=3 mice), suggesting that Pitx2+ SC neurons were specifically labeled in Pitx2-Cre mice (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a finding from validation of the Pitx2-Cre mouse line shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Most EGFP-expressing SC neurons in Pitx2-Cre mice were positive for vGlut2 mRNA (95 ± 7%, n=3 mice).
source: Moreover, most EGFP-expressing SC neurons were positive for vGlut2 mRNA (95 ± 7%, n=3 mice), and very few were positive for vGAT mRNA (6 ± 2.5%, n=3 mice), confirming that Pitx2+ SC neurons are predominantly glutamatergic (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is a finding from validation of the Pitx2-Cre mouse line shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Very few EGFP-expressing SC neurons in Pitx2-Cre mice were positive for vGAT mRNA (6 ± 2.5%, n=3 mice).
source: Moreover, most EGFP-expressing SC neurons were positive for vGlut2 mRNA (95 ± 7%, n=3 mice), and very few were positive for vGAT mRNA (6 ± 2.5%, n=3 mice), confirming that Pitx2+ SC neurons are predominantly glutamatergic (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is a finding from validation of the Pitx2-Cre mouse line shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons are predominantly glutamatergic.
source: Moreover, most EGFP-expressing SC neurons were positive for vGlut2 mRNA (95 ± 7%, n=3 mice), and very few were positive for vGAT mRNA (6 ± 2.5%, n=3 mice), confirming that Pitx2+ SC neurons are predominantly glutamatergic (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is an inference based on the high percentage of vGlut2+ and low percentage of vGAT+ cells.

claim: Synaptic inactivation of Pitx2+ SC neurons impaired prey capture.
source: Synaptic inactivation of Pitx2+ SC neurons impaired prey capture (Figure 3—video 2; Figure 3K) by increasing the latency to attack (Figure 3L), prolonging the time required for prey capture (Figure 3M), and reducing the frequency of attack (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3K-N.

claim: Synaptic inactivation of Pitx2+ SC neurons increased the latency to attack during prey capture.
source: Synaptic inactivation of Pitx2+ SC neurons impaired prey capture (Figure 3—video 2; Figure 3K) by increasing the latency to attack (Figure 3L), prolonging the time required for prey capture (Figure 3M), and reducing the frequency of attack (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Synaptic inactivation of Pitx2+ SC neurons prolonged the time required for prey capture.
source: Synaptic inactivation of Pitx2+ SC neurons impaired prey capture (Figure 3—video 2; Figure 3K) by increasing the latency to attack (Figure 3L), prolonging the time required for prey capture (Figure 3M), and reducing the frequency of attack (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Synaptic inactivation of Pitx2+ SC neurons reduced the frequency of attack during prey capture.
source: Synaptic inactivation of Pitx2+ SC neurons impaired prey capture (Figure 3—video 2; Figure 3K) by increasing the latency to attack (Figure 3L), prolonging the time required for prey capture (Figure 3M), and reducing the frequency of attack (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3N.

claim: The visually evoked freezing response was not impaired in mice with inactivated Pitx2+ SC neurons.
source: However, the visually evoked freezing response was not impaired in these mice, as evidenced by a lack of significant changes in locomotion speed before, during, or after the presentation of visual stimuli (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L–O).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L-O.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons are selectively required for prey capture behavior in mice.
source: These data suggest that Pitx2+ SC neurons are selectively required for prey capture behavior in mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing impaired hunting but not freezing.

claim: Rodents use vision to detect aerial predators.
source: Rodents use vision to detect aerial predators (De Franceschi et al., 2016; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), whereas they use vibrissal tactile information (Anjum et al., 2006) and vision (Hoy et al., 2016) for prey capture.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rodents use vibrissal tactile information and vision for prey capture.
source: Rodents use vision to detect aerial predators (De Franceschi et al., 2016; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), whereas they use vibrissal tactile information (Anjum et al., 2006) and vision (Hoy et al., 2016) for prey capture.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The centers of the visual RFs of Cbln2+ SC neurons were distributed predominantly in the dorsal quadrants of the visual field.
source: We found that the centers of the visual RFs of Cbln2+ SC neurons were distributed predominantly in the dorsal quadrants of the visual field (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons responded broadly to visual stimuli moving in various directions, with a preference for the temporal-to-nasal direction.
source: These neurons responded broadly to visual stimuli moving in various directions, with a preference for the temporal-to-nasal direction (Figure 4D,H).
evidence: This is a finding from fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 4D and 4H.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons responded more strongly to circles moving at lower velocity.
source: In addition, they responded more strongly to circles moving at lower velocity (Figure 4E,I) and those with smaller diameters (Figure 4F,J).
evidence: This is a finding from fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 4E and 4I.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons responded more strongly to circles with smaller diameters.
source: In addition, they responded more strongly to circles moving at lower velocity (Figure 4E,I) and those with smaller diameters (Figure 4F,J).
evidence: This is a finding from fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 4F and 4J.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons did not respond to air puffs applied to the vibrissal area.
source: However, the Cbln2+ SC neurons did not respond to air puffs applied to the vibrissal area (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons responded to air puffs directed toward the vibrissal region contralateral to the recorded side.
source: Unlike Cbln2+ SC neurons, Pitx2+ SC neurons responded to air puffs directed toward the vibrissal region contralateral to the recorded side (Figure 4G,K).
evidence: This is a finding from fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 4G and 4K.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons did not respond to moving visual stimuli.
source: However, they did not respond to moving visual stimuli (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is a finding from fiber photometry experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons may specifically process visual information derived from an aerial cruising predator.
source: These data indicate that Cbln2+ SC neurons may specifically process visual information derived from an aerial cruising predator, while Pitx2+ SC neurons may be selectively involved in processing vibrissal tactile stimuli mimicking moving prey.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensory response properties of Cbln2+ neurons.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons may be selectively involved in processing vibrissal tactile stimuli mimicking moving prey.
source: These data indicate that Cbln2+ SC neurons may specifically process visual information derived from an aerial cruising predator, while Pitx2+ SC neurons may be selectively involved in processing vibrissal tactile stimuli mimicking moving prey.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensory response properties of Pitx2+ neurons.

claim: Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ SC neurons may comprise two distinct sets of circuit modules that are used to detect visual cues produced by aerial predator and vibrissal cues produced by terrestrial prey of mice.
source: Thus, Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ SC neurons may comprise two distinct sets of circuit modules that are used to detect visual cues produced by aerial predator and vibrissal cues produced by terrestrial prey of mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensory response properties and behavioral roles of these neurons.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons were monosynaptically innervated by a subset of retinal ganglion cells in the contralateral retina.
source: First, Cbln2+ SC neurons were monosynaptically innervated by a subset of retinal ganglion cells in the contralateral retina (Figure 5D) and neurons in layer 5 of the ipsilateral primary visual cortex (V1) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons were monosynaptically innervated by neurons in layer 5 of the ipsilateral primary visual cortex (V1).
source: First, Cbln2+ SC neurons were monosynaptically innervated by a subset of retinal ganglion cells in the contralateral retina (Figure 5D) and neurons in layer 5 of the ipsilateral primary visual cortex (V1) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons did not receive monosynaptic inputs from retinal ganglion cells or V1.
source: In contrast, Pitx2+ SC neurons did not receive monosynaptic inputs from these visual structures (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons received robust monosynaptic inputs from the subnuclei of the trigeminal complex (Pr5 and Sp5).
source: Second, Pitx2+ SC neurons, but not Cbln2+ SC neurons, received robust monosynaptic inputs from the subnuclei of the trigeminal complex (Pr5 and Sp5) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (Figure 5G), and the ZI (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), which are involved in processing tactile information.
evidence: This is a finding from rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons received robust monosynaptic inputs from the primary somatosensory cortex (S1).
source: Second, Pitx2+ SC neurons, but not Cbln2+ SC neurons, received robust monosynaptic inputs from the subnuclei of the trigeminal complex (Pr5 and Sp5) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (Figure 5G), and the ZI (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), which are involved in processing tactile information.
evidence: This is a finding from rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons received robust monosynaptic inputs from the ZI.
source: Second, Pitx2+ SC neurons, but not Cbln2+ SC neurons, received robust monosynaptic inputs from the subnuclei of the trigeminal complex (Pr5 and Sp5) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (Figure 5G), and the ZI (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), which are involved in processing tactile information.
evidence: This is a finding from rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons did not receive monosynaptic inputs from Pr5, Sp5, S1, or ZI.
source: Second, Pitx2+ SC neurons, but not Cbln2+ SC neurons, received robust monosynaptic inputs from the subnuclei of the trigeminal complex (Pr5 and Sp5) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (Figure 5G), and the ZI (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), which are involved in processing tactile information.
evidence: This is a finding from rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5F-G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons received monosynaptic inputs from motor-related brain areas (e.g., SNr and M1/M2).
source: Third, Pitx2+ SC neurons, but not Cbln2+ SC neurons, also received monosynaptic inputs from motor-related brain areas (e.g., SNr and M1/M2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F) and the cingulate cortex (Cg1/2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons received monosynaptic inputs from the cingulate cortex (Cg1/2).
source: Third, Pitx2+ SC neurons, but not Cbln2+ SC neurons, also received monosynaptic inputs from motor-related brain areas (e.g., SNr and M1/M2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F) and the cingulate cortex (Cg1/2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ SC neurons may receive two sets of presynaptic inputs that are mutually exclusive.
source: Quantitative analysis of retrogradely labeled cells in various brain areas indicated that Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ SC neurons may receive two sets of presynaptic inputs that are mutually exclusive (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is an inference based on quantitative analysis of rabies virus tracing shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ SC neurons belong to two distinct sets of circuit modules that are used to detect visual cues produced by aerial predators (retina and V1) and tactile cues produced by terrestrial prey (Pr5, Sp5, S1, and ZI) of mice, respectively.
source: These morphological data support the hypothesis that Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ SC neurons belong to two distinct sets of circuit modules that are used to detect visual cues produced by aerial predators (retina and V1) and tactile cues produced by terrestrial prey (Pr5, Sp5, S1, and ZI) of mice, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the input connectivity data.

claim: Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ SC neurons sent divergent projections to a number of areas in the thalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla.
source: In addition to the LPTN and the ZI, Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ SC neurons sent divergent projections to a number of areas in the thalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is a finding from AAV tracing shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: The downstream target brain areas of Cbln2+ and Pitx2+ SC neurons rarely overlapped.
source: Strikingly, their downstream target brain areas rarely overlapped (Figure 6C–F), supporting the hypothesis that these two subtypes of SC neurons are functionally distinct.
evidence: This is a finding from AAV tracing shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: The density of EGFP+ axons from Cbln2+ SC neurons was significantly higher than that from Pitx2+ SC neurons in the LPTN.
source: Quantitative analyses of EGFP fluorescence indicated that the density of EGFP+ axons from Cbln2+ SC neurons was significantly higher than that from Pitx2+ SC neurons in the LPTN (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis of AAV tracing shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Cbln2+ SC neurons, but not Pitx2+ SC neurons, send strong projections to the LPTN.
source: These data suggest that Cbln2+ SC neurons, but not Pitx2+ SC neurons, send strong projections to the LPTN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative analysis of axon density.

claim: The density of EGFP+ axons from Pitx2+ SC neurons was significantly higher than that of EGFP+ axons from Cbln2+ SC neurons in the ZI.
source: Quantitative analysis of the EGFP fluorescence indicated that, in the ZI, the density of EGFP+ axons from Pitx2+ SC neurons was significantly higher than that of EGFP+ axons from Cbln2+ SC neurons (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative analysis of AAV tracing shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Pitx2+ SC neurons, but not Cbln2+ SC neurons, send strong projections to the ZI.
source: These data suggest that Pitx2+ SC neurons, but not Cbln2+ SC neurons, send strong projections to the ZI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative analysis of axon density.

claim: More than 80% of mCherry+ SC neurons (83 ± 9%, n=3 mice) in Cbln2-IRES-Cre mice were labeled by EGFP from retrograde AAV injected in LPTN.
source: More than 80% of mCherry+ SC neurons (83 ± 9%, n=3 mice) were labeled by EGFP, suggesting that a large proportion of Cbln2+ SC neurons project to the LPTN (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This is a finding from retrograde AAV tracing shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: A large proportion of Cbln2+ SC neurons project to the LPTN.
source: More than 80% of mCherry+ SC neurons (83 ± 9%, n=3 mice) were labeled by EGFP, suggesting that a large proportion of Cbln2+ SC neurons project to the LPTN (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the retrograde AAV tracing data.

claim: More than two-thirds of mCherry+ SC neurons (72 ± 11%, n=3 mice) in Pitx2-Cre mice were labeled by EGFP from retrograde AAV injected in ZI.
source: More than two-thirds of mCherry+ SC neurons (72 ± 11%, n=3 mice) were labeled by EGFP, suggesting that a large proportion of Pitx2+ neurons project to the ZI (Figure 7I–J).
evidence: This is a finding from retrograde AAV tracing shown in Figure 7I-J.

claim: A large proportion of Pitx2+ neurons project to the ZI.
source: More than two-thirds of mCherry+ SC neurons (72 ± 11%, n=3 mice) were labeled by EGFP, suggesting that a large proportion of Pitx2+ neurons project to the ZI (Figure 7I–J).
evidence: This is an inference based on the retrograde AAV tracing data.

claim: Light stimulation of ChR2-mCherry+ axon terminals of Cbln2+ SC neurons in the LPTN induced a freezing response in mice.
source: We found that light stimulation of ChR2-mCherry+ axon terminals of Cbln2+ SC neurons in the LPTN induced a freezing response in mice (Figure 8—video 1, Figure 8B–C), as evidenced by a selective reduction of locomotion speed during light stimulation (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8B-D.

claim: Activation of the Cbln2+ SC-LPTN pathway caused a selective reduction of locomotion speed during light stimulation.
source: We found that light stimulation of ChR2-mCherry+ axon terminals of Cbln2+ SC neurons in the LPTN induced a freezing response in mice (Figure 8—video 1, Figure 8B–C), as evidenced by a selective reduction of locomotion speed during light stimulation (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Activation of the Cbln2+ SC-LPTN pathway did not alter the efficiency of prey capture during predatory hunting.
source: However, activation of this pathway did not alter the efficiency of prey capture during predatory hunting (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Activation of the Cbln2+ SC-LPTN pathway selectively triggers predator avoidance rather than prey capture.
source: These data indicate that activation of the Cbln2+ SC-LPTN pathway selectively triggers predator avoidance rather than prey capture.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optogenetic behavioral data.

claim: Photostimulation of ChR2-mCherry+ axon terminals of Pitx2+ SC neurons in the ZI did not evoke a freezing response.
source: Photostimulation of ChR2-mCherry+ axon terminals of Pitx2+ SC neurons in the ZI did not evoke a freezing response (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is a finding from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: Activation of the Pitx2+ SC-ZI pathway promoted predatory hunting.
source: However, activation of this pathway promoted predatory hunting (Figure 8—video 2; Figure 8F–G) by decreasing the latency to hunt (Figure 8H), reducing the time required for prey capture (Figure 8I), and increasing the frequency of predatory attacks (Figure 8J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8F-J.

claim: Activation of the Pitx2+ SC-ZI pathway decreased the latency to hunt.
source: However, activation of this pathway promoted predatory hunting (Figure 8—video 2; Figure 8F–G) by decreasing the latency to hunt (Figure 8H), reducing the time required for prey capture (Figure 8I), and increasing the frequency of predatory attacks (Figure 8J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Activation of the Pitx2+ SC-ZI pathway reduced the time required for prey capture.
source: However, activation of this pathway promoted predatory hunting (Figure 8—video 2; Figure 8F–G) by decreasing the latency to hunt (Figure 8H), reducing the time required for prey capture (Figure 8I), and increasing the frequency of predatory attacks (Figure 8J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Activation of the Pitx2+ SC-ZI pathway increased the frequency of predatory attacks.
source: However, activation of this pathway promoted predatory hunting (Figure 8—video 2; Figure 8F–G) by decreasing the latency to hunt (Figure 8H), reducing the time required for prey capture (Figure 8I), and increasing the frequency of predatory attacks (Figure 8J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Activation of the Pitx2+ SC-ZI pathway selectively promotes prey capture without inducing predator avoidance.
source: These data indicate that activation of the Pitx2+ SC-ZI pathway selectively promotes prey capture without inducing predator avoidance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optogenetic behavioral data.

claim: The SC of the midbrain is a classical model for the study of early sensorimotor transformation related to sensory-triggered innate behaviors.
source: The SC of the midbrain is a classical model for the study of early sensorimotor transformation related to sensory-triggered innate behaviors (fish [Bianco and Engert, 2015]; rodents [Dean et al., 1989]; primates [Sparks, 1986]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations across multiple species.

claim: A series of projection-defined SC circuits have been linked to sensory-triggered innate behaviors such as predator avoidance and prey capture in mice.
source: In mice, a series of projection-defined SC circuits have been linked to sensory-triggered innate behaviors such as predator avoidance (Evans et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2019) and prey capture (Hoy et al., 2019; Shang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The number of cell types in the SC, their molecular signatures, their projection patterns, and their functional roles in behaviors remain unclear.
source: However, the number of cell types in the SC, their molecular signatures, their projection patterns, and their functional roles in these behaviors remain unclear.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Transcriptomically defined circuit modules correspond to specific behaviors in the midbrain.
source: First, they reveal that it is the transcriptomically defined neuronal subtypes and their projections, when combined together, define early sensorimotor transformation and the subsequent behavior. This finding supports the hypothesis that transcriptomically defined circuit modules correspond to specific behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration of all experimental data.

claim: Previous studies of the hypothalamus and prefrontal cortex did not find a clear correspondence between transcriptomically defined neurons and behaviors.
source: Previous studies of this 'correspondence' question in the hypothalamus and prefrontal cortex, two brain areas that are involved in the regulation of motivation and cognition, did not find a clear correspondence between transcriptomically defined neurons and behaviors (Kim et al., 2019; Lui et al., 2021; Moffitt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: The circuit design of sensorimotor transformation in the midbrain may differ from the circuit design in brain areas responsible for complex information processing such as motivation and cognition.
source: In combination with these pioneering studies, our results suggest that the circuit design of sensorimotor transformation in the midbrain, which requires precise detection of sensory features and rapid initiation of innate behaviors, may differ from the circuit design in brain areas that are responsible for complex information processing such as that related to the regulation of motivation and cognition.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: Cbln2 was extensively expressed by two subtypes of Op layer excitatory neurons.
source: Cbln2 was extensively expressed by two subtypes of Op layer excitatory neurons, but Pitx2 was expressed by only one subtype of InG layer excitatory neurons, indicating the heterogeneity of neurons located in different SC layers.
evidence: This is a finding from the transcriptomic analysis.

claim: Pitx2 was expressed by only one subtype of InG layer excitatory neurons.
source: Cbln2 was extensively expressed by two subtypes of Op layer excitatory neurons, but Pitx2 was expressed by only one subtype of InG layer excitatory neurons, indicating the heterogeneity of neurons located in different SC layers.
evidence: This is a finding from the transcriptomic analysis.

claim: Neurons with similar transcriptomic profiles may tend to participate in the same projection paths and to play a role in the regulation of behavior.
source: Our data also suggest that neurons with similar transcriptomic profiles may tend to participate in the same projection paths and to play a role in the regulation of behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between transcriptomic profiles and projection patterns.

claim: Cbln2 and other members of the Cerebellin family are synaptic organizer molecules that bind to presynaptic neurexins and to postsynaptic receptors.
source: Cbln2 and other members of the Cerebellin family are synaptic organizer molecules that bind to presynaptic neurexins and to postsynaptic receptors (Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Cbln2 may participate in synapse formation.
source: Recent studies have shown that Cbln2 may participate in synapse formation (Matsuda and Yuzaki, 2011; Seigneur and Südhof, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pitx2 participates in the migration of collicular neurons during brain development.
source: As a transcription factor, Pitx2 participates in the migration of collicular neurons during brain development (Waite et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Activation of Pitx2+ SC neurons elicited stereotyped head displacements in a body-referenced frame.
source: In the adult brain, activation of Pitx2+ SC neurons elicited stereotyped head displacements in a body-referenced frame (Masullo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.
